import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram,linkage
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder,StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.metrics import (silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_score,
                             calinski_harabasz_score,adjusted_rand_score)
from kneed import KneeLocator

os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"


R_S = 42 # random state
RED = '#CC0000'
plt.rcParams.update({
    'axes.titlecolor': RED, 'axes.titleweight': 'bold', 'axes.titlesize': 13,
    'axes.edgecolor': RED, 'axes.labelsize': 11, 'figure.dpi': 100,
})
sns.set_style("whitegrid")

os.makedirs('screenshots',exist_ok = True)

def knee_point(x, y):
    # Point on the curve farthest from the straight line joining its two ends
    x = (np.asarray(x) - np.min(x)) / (np.max(x) - np.min(x))
    y = (np.asarray(y) - np.min(y)) / (np.max(y) - np.min(y))
    dist = np.abs((y[-1] - y[0]) * x - (x[-1] - x[0]) * y + x[-1] * y[0] - y[-1] * x[0])
    return int(np.argmax(dist))

def save_fig(name):
    plt.savefig(f"screenshots/{name}.png",dpi=150,bbox_inches="tight")

def cluster_palette(name, labels):
    labels = sorted(set(labels) - {-1})
    return dict(zip(labels, sns.color_palette(name, len(labels))))

1.6 EDA Summary¶

  • Observations :
    • Age is right-skewed with most customers between their 20s and 40s.
    • Annual Income is also right skewed (long tail up to ~135 k$).
    • Spending Score is roughly bell shaped around 50 with no extreme shew.
    • which motivates scaling.
  • Correlation are weak :
    • the moderate relationship is Age vs Spending_Score(r = -0.33) - younger customers tend to score higher
    • Annual_Income vs Spending_score has r= 0.01.
    • Gender is essentially uncorrelated with everything(|r| < 0.06).
  • why a near-zero correalation does not mean "no structure":
    • Pearson correlation only measures linear trend.in The Annual_Income vs spending_Score panel of the pairplot the points form about five distinct blobs(noe in each corner plus a dense group in the centre),so the relationship is grouped rather than linear- exactly what clustering is designed to find.

  • 2.3 why Scaling is needed
    • why StandardScaler before clustering?
      • K-Means,Hierarchical and DBSCAN are all Distance-based : they decide cluster membership by Euckidean dustance between points. A feature with a large numeric range contributes more to that distance
  • Raw Annual_Income spans roughly 15-137, whereas Spanding_Score spans 1-100 and Age spans 18-70. Unscaled,income differences would dominate every distance calculation and the cluster would mostly reflect income alone.
  • StandaedScaler rewrite each feature as z= (x-mean)/std, giving every feature mean 0 and std 1, so each contributes on an equal footing.
  • Gender is not scaled because is already a 0/1 binary variable.

What is inertia? :

  • Inertia is sum of squred distances between every point and the centroid of its assigned cluster(the within-cluster sum of squares). lower inertia means tighter clusters

Why does the elbow indicate a good k? :

  • Inertia always decreases as k grows (at k=200 it would ne 0, with every customer in its own cluster).
  • Going from 1 --> 5 clusters removes large amounts of inertia because each new cluster captures a henuinely separate group.
  • After the elbow, each extra cluster only splits an already-compact group and the fains necome marginal.
  • The elbow os the point of diminidhing returns -- here at k=5, where the curve flattens

Segment names and business implications

Segment Profile Business implication for the marketing team
High Income, High Spenders Younger (~33), income ≈ 87 k$, score ≈ 82 The most valuable group: they have both the means and the willingness to spend. Protect and grow with premium offers and loyalty.
Low Income, High Spenders Youngest (~25), income ≈ 26 k$, score ≈ 79 Enthusiastic but budget-limited shoppers. Respond to deals, trends and instalment offers; at risk of over-stretching.
High Income, Low Spenders Middle-aged (~41), income ≈ 88 k$, score ≈ 17 Large untapped potential: money is available but the mall is not capturing it. Need a reason to visit and spend.
Low Income, Low Spenders Oldest (~45), income ≈ 26 k$, score ≈ 21 Spend little by necessity and are price-sensitive. Low-cost retention only; do not over-invest.
Mid Income, Mid Spenders Middle-aged (~43), income ≈ 55 k$, score ≈ 50 The largest, "average" segment (about 40 % of customers). Steady revenue base; nudge up with general promotions and upsell.

Task 4: Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering¶

In [17]:
# 4.1 Dendrogram
z = linkage(df_2f,method="ward")
heights = z[:,2]
gaps = np.diff(heights)
largest_gap = int(np.argmax(gaps))
cut_height = (heights[largest_gap]+heights[largest_gap+1])/2
n_hier = len(df_2f) - (largest_gap+1)

plt.figure(figsize=(14,6))
dendrogram(z,color_threshold=cut_height,no_labels=True,above_threshold_color="grey")
plt.axhline(cut_height,color=RED,linestyle="--",linewidth = 2,
            label=f"Optimal Cut (height = {cut_height:.2f}) -> {n_hier} clusters")
plt.title("Dendrogram - Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (ward Linkage)")
plt.xlabel("Customers (each leaf is one Clusters)")
plt.ylabel("Ward linkage distance")
plt.legend(loc="upper right")
save_fig("08_dendrogram")
plt.show()
print(f"Longest vertical gap = {gaps[largest_gap]:.2f} -> cut at {cut_height:.2f} -> {n_hier} clusters")

Longest vertical gap = 5.10 -> cut at 6.90 -> 5 clusters

What does Ward linkage minimise? At every step, Ward merges the pair of clusters whose union causes the smallest increase in total within-cluster variance (sum of squared distances to the cluster centroid). It is the hierarchical analogue of K-Means' inertia objective, so it tends to build compact, similarly sized clusters.

How to read the dendrogram and choose the number of clusters

  • The x-axis shows individual customers; the y-axis is the Ward distance at which clusters merge. Low merges join near-identical customers; high merges join very different groups.
  • Look for the longest vertical line that is not crossed by any horizontal merge. A long vertical line means the algorithm had to jump a large distance to merge the next pair, i.e. those clusters are genuinely distinct.
  • Draw a horizontal cut through that gap and count how many vertical lines it crosses. Here the largest gap lies between heights ≈ 4.4 and ≈ 9.4, so the cut at ≈ 6.9 crosses 5 branches → 5 clusters, matching K-Means.

# 4.2 Fit Agglomerative model
agg = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=n_hier,linkage='ward').fit(df_2f)

overlap = pd.crosstab(agg.labels_,df["KMeans_Cluster"])
rows,cols = linear_sum_assignment(-overlap.values)
label_map = dict(zip(overlap.index[rows],overlap.columns[cols]))
df["Hier_Cluster"] = pd.Series(agg.labels_,index=df.index).map(label_map)
print(df["Hier_Cluster"].value_counts().sort_index().rename("Customers"))

Do the cluster boundaries agree? Yes, very strongly. The two algorithms produce essentially the same five segments (Adjusted Rand Index ≈ 0.94); only the few circled customers are assigned differently. All of them lie in the border regions between touching clusters — mainly between the large central group and the High-Income/Low-Spend group, and between the central group and the Low-Income/High-Spend group.

Why do border customers differ?

  • K-Means is centroid-based: every point goes to the nearest centroid, which creates straight, equidistant (Voronoi) boundaries. A border point simply joins whichever cenatre is closer right now.
  • Hierarchical (Ward) is connectivity/merge-based: points are assigned by the order in which clusters were merged bottom-up, so a border point stays with the sub-cluster it was joined to early on, even if another cluster's centroid is slightly closer. The final clusters are also not forced to have centroid-optimal boundaries.
  • Where clusters are well separated both methods agree perfectly; they only diverge where groups touch.

Task 5: DBSCAN Clustering¶

In [45]:
# 5.1 Parameter tuning - epsilon
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=4).fit(df_2f)
distances,_ = nn.kneighbors(df_2f)
k_dist = np.sort(distances[:, -1])
knee_idx = knee_point(np.arange(len(k_dist)),k_dist)
eps_suggested = k_dist[knee_idx]

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(k_dist, color=RED, linewidth=2, label='4-NN distance')
plt.axhline(eps_suggested, color='black', linestyle='--', label=f'Knee ≈ {eps_suggested:.2f}')
plt.scatter([knee_idx], [eps_suggested], s=120, facecolors='none', edgecolors='black', linewidths=2)
plt.title('4-NN Distance Plot — Estimating DBSCAN eps')
plt.xlabel('Points sorted by distance')
plt.ylabel('Distance to 4th nearest neighbour')
plt.legend()
save_fig('11_knn_distance_plot')
plt.show()
print(f'Suggested eps from the knee: {eps_suggested:.3f}')

Suggested eps from the knee: 0.313

Each point's distance to its 4th nearest neighbour (counting itself, which matches how DBSCAN counts min_samples) is sorted from smallest to largest. Most points sit in dense areas and have small, slowly increasing distances; the curve then bends sharply upward for isolated points. The automatic knee detector marks the start of the bend at eps ≈ 0.31, and the curve rises steeply beyond roughly 0.4, where the remaining points are increasingly isolated. The recommended range is therefore about 0.3–0.5, which is explored in the grid search below.

# 5.2 Grid Search - eps & min_samples

records =[]
for eps in eps_values:
    for ms in min_samples_values:
        labels = DBSCAN(eps=eps,min_samples=ms).fit_predict(df_2f)
        core = labels != -1
        n_clusters = len(set(labels[core]))
        sil = silhouette_score(df_2f[core], labels[core]) if n_clusters > 1 else np.nan
        records.append({'eps': eps, 'min_samples': ms, 'n_clusters': n_clusters,
                        'n_noise': int((~core).sum()), 'silhouette': round(sil, 3)})

grid = pd.DataFrame(records)
grid.style.format({'silhouette': '{:.3f}'}, na_rep='n/a (<2 clusters)').background_gradient(cmap='Reds', subset=['n_noise'])

Choosing the parameters. The goal is coherent clusters with minimal noise:

  • eps = 0.2: with min_samples ≥ 4 the silhouettes look excellent (≈ 0.59–0.62) but are misleading — 73–95 of 200 customers (up to 47 %) are labelled noise, so only the densest cores are scored. With min_samples = 3 the data splits into 13 tiny clusters.
  • eps = 0.3: fragments the data into 6–9 small clusters with 14–48 noise points; groups that belong together are split.
  • eps = 0.5–0.6: too large; everything merges into 1–2 clusters.
  • eps = 0.4: the sweet spot, just above the detected knee (≈ 0.31) where the 4-NN curve starts to climb steeply. With min_samples = 5 it finds 4 clusters, only 15 noise points (7.5 %) and a silhouette of ≈ 0.48, a better silhouette than min_samples = 4 for almost the same noise.

Selected: eps = 0.4, min_samples = 5.

What eps and min_samples control

  • eps is the neighbourhood radius: two points are neighbours if they are within eps of each other (in scaled units). A small eps gives many small clusters and lots of noise; a large eps merges neighbouring clusters.
  • min_samples is the number of points (including the point itself) required inside that radius for a point to be a core point. Higher values demand denser regions, so more points become noise.
  • A cluster is a set of core points connected through overlapping neighbourhoods, plus the border points that lie within eps of a core point.

Why noise points arise: a point that is neither a core point nor within eps of one is too far from any dense region to belong to a cluster. Here they are the black × markers — mostly customers in the sparse outer areas of the plot — 12 of the 15 belong to the two high-income segments (see the cross-tab in 5.5).

Adjusted Rand Index (K-Means vs DBSCAN, noise as its own group): 0.568

DBSCAN vs K-Means

  1. Number of clusters: DBSCAN does not need k upfront — it infers the number of clusters from density (4 here). K-Means must be told k, which we estimated with Elbow/Silhouette.
  2. Cluster shape: DBSCAN can find arbitrarily shaped clusters (crescents, rings, elongated chains) because it follows density-connected points. K-Means assumes compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size.
  3. Outliers: DBSCAN labels low-density points as noise; K-Means forces every point into a cluster, so outliers pull centroids.
  4. Do all three algorithms agree on the number of segments? Not entirely. K-Means and Hierarchical both find 5, but DBSCAN finds 4 plus noise. The cross-tab shows why: the Low-Income/High-Spenders points are density-connected to the central group, and part of the Low-Income/Low-Spenders group is as well, so DBSCAN absorbs them into one big central cluster — it sees one continuous dense region where K-Means sees several groups.
  5. Most stable segments across all three algorithms: High Income / High Spenders and High Income / Low Spenders (compact, isolated blobs that every method recovers almost identically), plus the large Mid / Mid core. The least stable are the low-income groups and the customers on cluster borders.

def evaluate(name, data, labels):
    mask = labels != -1
    return {'Algorithm': name,
            'n_clusters': len(set(labels[mask])),
            'Noise points': int((~mask).sum()),
            'Silhouette Score': silhouette_score(data[mask], labels[mask]),
            'Davies-Bouldin Index': davies_bouldin_score(data[mask], labels[mask]),
            'Calinski-Harabasz Index': calinski_harabasz_score(data[mask], labels[mask])}

metrics = pd.DataFrame([
    evaluate('K-Means', df_2f, df['KMeans_Cluster'].to_numpy()),
    evaluate('Agglomerative (Ward)', df_2f, df['Hier_Cluster'].to_numpy()),
    evaluate('DBSCAN (noise excluded)', df_2f, df['DBSCAN_Cluster'].to_numpy()),
]).set_index('Algorithm')

 .highlight_max(subset=['Silhouette Score', 'Calinski-Harabasz Index'], color='#f8c9c9')
 .highlight_min(subset=['Davies-Bouldin Index'], color='#f8c9c9')

Which algorithm performs best and why?

  • K-Means scores best on all three metrics (Silhouette ≈ 0.555, Davies-Bouldin ≈ 0.572, Calinski-Harabasz ≈ 248.7), with Hierarchical practically tied (0.554 / 0.578 / 244.4) — the two find nearly identical partitions.
  • DBSCAN scores lower (Silhouette ≈ 0.478, Davies-Bouldin ≈ 0.591, Calinski-Harabasz ≈ 146.9) because it merged several segments into one large central cluster, which lowers separation. Its scores are also computed only on the non-noise points, so they are not strictly comparable with the other two.
  • Caveat: all three metrics reward compact, convex, well-separated clusters, which is the kind of structure K-Means produces, so they are naturally biased in its favour. On this dataset the five blobs are roughly spherical, so that bias is harmless here — but the metrics measure geometry, not business usefulness.

Business Insights for Mall Management¶

(a) Customer segments identified by K-Means (the most interpretable result)¶

  1. High Income, High Spenders (19.5 %) — younger affluent shoppers (avg. age ≈ 33, income ≈ 87 k$, score ≈ 82). The mall's "stars."
  2. Low Income, High Spenders (11 %) — the youngest group (≈ 25), modest income (≈ 26 k$) but very high spending score (≈ 79). Trend-driven and impulsive.
  3. High Income, Low Spenders (17.5 %) — middle-aged (≈ 41), high income (≈ 88 k$) but low score (≈ 17). Cautious, selective or shopping elsewhere.
  4. Low Income, Low Spenders (11.5 %) — oldest group (≈ 45), low income (≈ 26 k$) and low score (≈ 21). Budget-constrained and price-sensitive.
  5. Mid Income, Mid Spenders (40.5 %) — the largest, "average" group (income ≈ 55 k$, score ≈ 50).

(b) One targeted marketing action per segment¶

Segment Recommended action
High Income, High Spenders Premium loyalty programme: tiered rewards, early access to new collections, VIP lounge/personal-shopper events to protect share of wallet.
Low Income, High Spenders Budget-friendly promotions: student/young-adult discount days, flash sales, buy-now-pay-later and trend-focused pop-ups, with a points system rewarding frequent visits.
High Income, Low Spenders Experience-led re-engagement: curated luxury/premium brand launches, fine dining, personalised invitations and concierge services to give them a reason to spend here. Survey them to find out what is missing.
Low Income, Low Spenders Low-cost value offers: coupon booklets, essentials-focused discounts and free community events to maintain footfall without heavy marketing spend.
Mid Income, Mid Spenders Broad upsell campaigns: seasonal sales, bundle deals and a simple entry-level loyalty card to nudge this large base up towards the high-spend segments.

(c) Recommended algorithm for deployment¶

K-Means is recommended for production: it gives the best (or joint-best) metrics, finds five clear, well-balanced segments, assigns every customer to a segment (a marketing team needs an action for everyone), is fast, and produces centroids that translate directly into easy-to-explain segment profiles. New customers can also be assigned instantly with kmeans.predict.

The alternatives are still useful in specific situations: Hierarchical clustering is the best choice for management presentations because the dendrogram shows how segments nest and merge; DBSCAN is best when cluster shapes are unknown or when flagging unusual customers (outliers) matters. Because K-Means and Hierarchical agree on ~94 % of the structure, the segmentation can be trusted as stable.
